lesson_title: The Water Truck That Runs a Continent
hook_text: Richards Bay: green and muggy. Alexander Bay: bare desert. Same latitude. Blame the pots.
clip_script: Imagine one enormous water truck that drives a single north-south road across Africa, spraying rain as it goes. The truck is the ITCZ — the band where the two hemispheres' trade winds crash together and hurl air upward into thunderstorms. Wherever the truck is parked, it is pouring. And it keeps a strict timetable, chasing the overhead sun about a month behind. In January it parks at the southern end of its route, hosing Angola, Zambia and Zimbabwe and splashing the far north of South Africa. In July it has driven to the far northern end to water the Sahel, while everything down here waits, dry, in the winter sun. Your rainfall calendar is just how often the truck passes your gate: live at the middle of the route, like the Congo Basin, and it passes twice a year — two rainy seasons. Live near the ends, like Zimbabwe or Mali, and it barely reaches you once. Now feel the danger: if the truck runs late one year, or turns back early, the end-of-route customers get nothing at all. That is what most tropical droughts are — not a broken sky, just a truck that never quite arrived. Whole harvests hang on the last fifty kilometres of that route, and now you can see it coming on any satellite image.
visual_style: A glowing storm band drawn as a truck route down a map of Africa, headlights sliding north and south as months tick past, gardens greening as it passes and browning as it leaves, ending on a stalled truck short of a waiting farm.
mood: Playful metaphor tightening into real continental stakes.
pacing: Easy build through the timetable, quick two-pass beat, slow sober close on the missed delivery.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any African climate off the circulation for yourself.
